summary: Defines the underlying data model used by SIMPLE presence agents for SIP-based instant messaging and presence. It guides mapping different communication systems into presence documents consistently. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A shared way of describing whether someone is around, such as online, busy or away, so different chat programs can understand each other.

subtitle: A way to say what a presence document describes: a person, the services that reach them, and the devices those services run on.

tldr.problem: Earlier presence specifications modeled presence as a list of tuples but never said what a tuple stands for, or how to map real communications systems, especially SIP-based ones, into a presence document.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC splits a presentity into three kinds of component: one person, any number of services and any number of devices. Each carries its own characteristics and status, and is written into a PIDF document with new person and device elements beside the existing tuple.
tldr.outcome: Presence documents describe people, services and devices consistently, and older PIDF software that does not know the new elements can still read them.

facts.label: Recommended device ID
facts.value: UUID URN (version 1 with a MAC, otherwise version 4)

today: RFC 4479 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Gap in Earlier Presence Specs
sections.content:
Presence conveys the ability and willingness of a user to communicate across a set of devices. RFC 2778 defines a model and terminology for presence, and RFC 3863 defines an XML format, the Presence Information Data Format (PIDF), for it. Both model presence as a series of tuples, each holding a status, a communications address and other markup.

Neither document says what a tuple is meant to model, or how to map real-world communications systems, especially those built on SIP, into a presence document. RFC 4479 fills that gap with three named concepts: a service (such as instant messaging or telephony), a device (a phone, PDA or PC) and a person (the end user, with states such as busy or sad). The data model is defined as an extension to RFC 3863.
sections.eli5: People had a form for saying how to reach someone, but nobody said what each box on the form meant. This RFC labels the boxes: the person, the ways to talk, and the gadgets.

sections.title: Presentity, Person, Service and Device
sections.content:
The model describes a presentity, identified by a presentity URI. It has three kinds of data component: person, service and device. Each holds attributes, which are either characteristics (usually fixed and descriptive) or status (information that typically changes).

The key rule is that an attribute belongs to the thing it describes, not to the thing that reported it. If a cell phone reports that the user is in a meeting, the attribute goes in the person component with a status of in-a-meeting, because that is a fact about the human, not about the phone.

There can be only one person component per presentity, though it may appear in several occurrences when the state is ambiguous. The person is a facade for a single person: a help desk could be modeled as one person who is busy when no staff are free.

The presentity URI is the identifier for the presentity. A presentity may have several, for example a URI from the pres scheme and a SIP URI. It should ideally be set to the identifier used to request the document, and it is a resource that can be subscribed to.
sections.eli5: A fact goes on the card of whoever it is true about. If your phone says you are in a meeting, that goes on your card, not the phone's card, because you are the one in the meeting.

sections.title: How Services Are Described
sections.content:
A service is a point of reachability for communications, such as telephony, push-to-talk, instant messaging, SMS or MMS. The RFC admits that service is hard to define precisely, so it does not enumerate services and keeps no central registry. Anything counts as a service if it has the key properties below.

  • Characteristics describe the nature and capabilities of the service. They matter most when several services are listed, because listing several gives the watcher a choice.
  • Reach information says how to contact the service. It usually includes a service URI, and it works as a unique identifier for the service. Something cannot be its own service unless it can be reached separately. A softphone that does audio and video is one service, because there is no way to reach a video-only part.
  • Relative information is a priority, which only has meaning relative to other services. Priorities of 1 and .5 are the same as .2 and .1.
  • Status includes the basic status, either open or closed. Closed means communication will in all likelihood fail or not reach the intended party.

Reach information is a weak contract, not a guarantee, and the preferences of the presentity always take precedence. A watcher that receives reach information it does not understand should discard that service. A document may even list a service with no reach information, to show that it exists without offering a way to connect. Dynamic state is included only when it helps a watcher decide whether or when to communicate; signal strength does not qualify.
sections.eli5: Each way to reach you gets its own entry: what it is like, exactly how to dial it, which one you like best, and whether it works right now. The list is a menu, not an order.

sections.title: Devices, Ambiguity and Absent Data
sections.content:
Devices model the physical environment in which services run, such as cell phones, PCs, PDAs and PBX extensions. Services and devices map many to many: two SIP phones can register against one address of record, and one cell phone can run SIP telephony, SMS and MMS services. A device with no services, like an RFID tag, can still carry properties such as location that a compositor combines with other documents.

Each device has a device ID, a URN that should be unique, persistent and easy to compute. No suitable URN scheme existed yet, so the RFC recommends the UUID URN: version 1 for devices with a MAC address, version 4 for devices without one. The device ID lets services be correlated to the device they share, even if the device information is filtered out of the document. Device status has no bearing on a service unless the consumer knows otherwise; any effect is expressed by adjusting the service state.

Ambiguity is modeled explicitly. Any service, device or person can have multiple occurrences, each with a unique occurrence identifier. A watcher, or a human, may resolve ambiguity better than the compositor. The timestamp and note help, and the most recently changed source can be treated as more reliable, though that rule is not normative.

The absence of an attribute says nothing definitive, so a document should carry as many attributes as the presentity is willing and able to provide (RECOMMENDED). The status/characteristic split is only conceptual. Future attributes MUST be defined as children of <tuple>, not of <status>.
sections.eli5: Gadgets get ID tags so the system knows when two apps live on the same phone. If two reports disagree, the card can keep both and let the reader decide. A missing item means "no comment", not "no".

sections.title: Encoding in PIDF
sections.content:
The model is written in PIDF. The <presence> element holds the presentity, with its entity attribute set to the presentity URI. The existing <tuple> element represents a service, with <contact> carrying the service URI and the tuple id giving the service occurrence. Older attributes such as <basic> stay under <status> for compatibility; a service attribute appears in one place or the other, never both.

The RFC adds two elements under <presence>, each allowed zero or more times and in any order. <person> and <device> each have a mandatory id attribute holding the occurrence identifier. Both contain status and characteristic elements, then optional <note> elements and an optional <timestamp>. A <device> also holds a required <deviceID>. Notes directly under <presence> apply to any person occurrence that has none of its own.

Clients that do not implement this specification ignore the new elements, so documents stay compatible with older implementations. Documents MUST be valid, except that a compositor may produce one that only validates under lax processing. Receivers SHOULD be ready to extract what they can from documents that are not valid. Two XML schemas, a common schema and a data-model schema, define the types and elements.
sections.eli5: The new card is the old card with two extra pockets, one for the person and one for each gadget. Old readers just skip the new pockets.

sections.title: Extension Rules and a Worked Example
sections.content:
Anyone adding a presence attribute must ask whether it applies to person, service or device and what it means in each, and whether it belongs in a new or existing namespace. If the extension is itself extensible, its points of extension MUST be defined in the schema, and SHOULD use the any namespace="##other" construct. Geographic location shows the point. It fits a person or a device but not a service, so <geopriv> objects SHOULD go under person or device, though receivers SHOULD still accept them under <tuple> as an earlier RFC advised.

The worked example is a basic instant messaging client. The person component carries the user's note and status, the service tuple represents the IM service with the client's address of record as the service URI, and a device component models the PC. The idle indicator goes on the device, since idleness describes use of the machine. That lets a presence server combine it with other services on the same device: a user on a VoIP call is plainly using a device whose keyboard is idle.
sections.eli5: If you invent a new kind of fact, you have to decide whose card it belongs on. "Is the computer idle?" belongs on the computer's card, because it is about the computer.

sections.title: Security and Internationalization
sections.content:
Presence information is very sensitive, so privacy filtering, which means removing whatever a watcher is not authorized to see, plays a key role. The SIP presence specifications require that authorization be performed before presence is divulged, and filtering can even hide from the presentity that a watcher is blocked. Integrity matters too, since an attacker who modifies presence data can divert communications. The RFC relies on the transport, such as SIP, for integrity.

The model is mostly tokens meant for programs, which translate them for the watcher. Free-text <note> elements SHOULD carry an xml:lang attribute, with a default of i-default, and repeating the note allows several languages. UTF-8 is RECOMMENDED where parsers disagree on encodings.
sections.eli5: Where you are and what you are doing is private, so the system must check who is allowed to read your card and make sure nobody scribbles on it.

viz.caption: THE THREE DATA COMPONENTS OF A PRESENTITY

items.title: Person
items.text: The human user and the states that affect willingness to communicate. Only one per presentity.

items.title: Service
items.text: A point of reachability such as telephony or instant messaging, with characteristics, reach information, priority and status.

items.title: Device
items.text: The physical environment where services run, identified by a device ID URN.
